poll.decodersHeading: Three ideas you need for the Data Lab

decoders.title: Dementia is the symptoms. Alzheimer’s disease is one cause.
decoders.body: Dementia describes a set of symptoms, such as memory loss and confusion, that are bad enough to affect daily life. Alzheimer’s disease is a specific disease of the brain and the most common cause of dementia. Scientists recognise it by changes in brain tissue that can be seen under a microscope.

decoders.title: Selective cellular vulnerability
decoders.body: The brain has many types of cell, and a disease does not have to affect them all equally. Asking which cell types change, and how early, is one of the main questions in the Data Lab. PLACEHOLDER: one sentence on what is known for Alzheimer’s disease, from a subject expert.

decoders.title: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing, in A-level terms
decoders.body: Every cell carries the same DNA, but each cell type transcribes a different set of genes into mRNA. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) counts the mRNA molecules in one nucleus at a time. That tells you which genes were switched on in that cell, and the pattern tells you what type of cell it is.

cheats.title: Correlation vs causation
cheats.body: Two things changing together does not show that one causes the other. Something else may cause both, or the cause may run the other way.

cheats.title: Sample size
cheats.body: A pattern in 5 donors could be chance. Check the n under each group: the fewer the donors, the less weight a difference can carry.

cheats.title: Confounding variables
cheats.body: If the groups differ in age, sex or genes as well as in disease stage, any of those could explain the difference. Split the data by the confounder and see if the pattern survives.

cheats.title: Limits of post-mortem tissue
cheats.body: Each brain is measured once, after death. You see one moment per person, never the same person changing over time, so you cannot watch a disease progress.

cheats.title: mRNA is not protein
cheats.body: snRNA-seq measures transcription. More mRNA usually means more protein, but not always: translation and protein breakdown are controlled separately.

lab.observeMatch: In this data the median is {{trend}} in the last group than the first. That matches your prediction.
lab.observeMiss: In this data the median is {{trend}} in the last group than the first. You predicted {{prediction}}. A prediction that fails is still useful: it tells you something you believed needs another look.
lab.observeNoPrediction: In this data the median is {{trend}} in the last group than the first.
lab.stressIntro: The groups might differ in more than disease stage. Pick a variable and split every group by it. If the pattern holds in each split, that variable is less likely to explain it.
lab.stressCountsHeading: How the donors fall across groups
lab.stressCountsNote: If one column is mostly one kind of donor, that variable is tangled up with the grouping.

ucas.heading: UCAS and careers
ucas.intro: Nobody is born knowing how university applications work. Here is the part people rarely say out loud.
ucas.statementIntro: Admissions tutors want to know what you did and what you learned, not that you found it interesting.
ucas.weak: I did an online project about Alzheimer’s and found it interesting.
ucas.strong: Investigating single-nucleus transcriptomic data from the SEA-AD atlas, I analysed the selective vulnerability of SST inhibitory interneurons across Braak stages, developing skills in evaluating donor spread and confounding variables.
statementWhy: It names the data and the method.
It says exactly what was analysed.
It ends on a skill, not a feeling.
ucas.statementWarning: Do not copy this sentence. UCAS checks every application for matching text and tells universities what it finds. Write about what you actually did, in your own words.
ucas.compHeading: Beyond medicine: what is computational biology?
comp: Biomedical research is not only doctors and people in lab coats with pipettes. A growing share of it is done at a computer.
Computational biologists write code to find patterns in large biological datasets, like the one on this site. The same skills are used in bioinformatics, health data science and AI in healthcare.
You can reach it from biology, biochemistry, biomedical science, maths, computer science or physics. Entry requirements differ by course, so check each one on the UCAS course search.
founder: PLACEHOLDER [GIULIO]: a short personal note. What you did not know at 17, and why research is a series of steps anyone can learn.

teachers.heading: For teachers
teachers.intro: A free 50-minute workshop on Alzheimer’s disease and gene expression for Year 12 and 13, built on research data.
value: Runs in the browser on a standard school Chromebook. No accounts and no software.
After the first load it keeps working if the school Wi-Fi drops.
One lesson: warm-up poll, guided data simulations, then independent exploration.
The essay prize is optional follow-up work.

topics: 3.6 Organisms respond to changes in their internal and external environments (nervous coordination, synapses)
Module 5: Communication, homeostasis and energy (neuronal communication)
Module 6: Genetics, evolution and ecosystems (manipulating genomes)
